lead: An automated biochemical analyser pipettes sample and reagent, incubates at 37 °C, reads absorbance and computes concentration for hundreds of tests an hour. A hospital laboratory may receive 500 samples before noon, each needing several tests; a bench cuvette cannot keep up. The chemistry is still the Beer–Lambert law; only pipetting, timing and washing are mechanised.
prereq: Read Chapter 3.1 for the Beer–Lambert law, the cuvette photometer and calibration.

sections.h3: The fluid path and the blocks

blocks.text: A sample probe dips into the tube, senses liquid level and aspirates 2–20 µL of serum. A second probe adds 200–300 µL of reagent. Capacitive sensing: the probe tip is one plate of a capacitor, and capacitance changes when the tip touches serum. Resistive sensing: the probe and grounded tube form a circuit whose conductance changes when the tip enters conducting serum. Either change stops the downward drive and flags a short sample.
Two pumps move liquids. A peristaltic pump squeezes a flexible tube with rollers; it is cheap but less precise. A syringe pump drives a piston and delivers microlitre volumes accurately.

The mixture enters a cuvette in a wheel held at 37 °C for a fixed incubation time. Light from the lamp passes through the filter wheel, which selects the wavelength — common ones are 340, 405, 505, 546, 578 and 600 nm — then through the cuvette. A photodiode after the cuvette measures transmitted light. A wash station aspirates the used mixture and rinses the cuvette.

Continuous-flow or air-segmented analysers push sample and reagent as one stream broken by air bubbles. The bubbles scrub the tube wall and keep samples apart as the stream passes one detector. Every sample gets the same timing. Very few remain installed.

Discrete analysers give each test its own cuvette. In a random-access analyser any test can be ordered on any sample at any time, and an emergency sample can jump the queue; most large Indian laboratories use these. A batch analyser runs one test on a long row of samples and is cheaper for one high-volume assay.

Throughput is quoted in tests per hour. 600 tests per hour means one result every 3600 s ÷ 600 = 6 s on average. This is cycle time, not the incubation time of one test, which is longer and overlaps other tests. A probe washed between samples still carries a trace of previous reagent, so reagent carryover adds a small false rise to the next result. Daily quality control uses control sera of known value on a chart with ±2 SD limits.

sections.h3: Reading the result: end point, kinetic, bichromatic

blocks.text: A reagent starts the reaction and absorbance changes. In an end-point assay the reaction runs to completion and the analyser reads the final absorbance once. The computer converts it with a stored calibration curve:

blocks.where: c(sample) is the unknown concentration in mmol/L; c(std) is the calibrator value in mmol/L; A(sample) and A(std) are net absorbances, meaning measured absorbance minus reagent blank and cuvette blank: A = A(measured) − A(blank).

blocks.text: In a kinetic assay the analyser takes several readings while the reaction runs at a steady rate and computes ΔA/min, the change in absorbance per minute. Enzyme tests are usually read as a rate, because activity is proportional to ΔA/min; some fixed-time methods read one absorbance after a set incubation, but a true rate method cannot be read as an end point.

Bichromatic measurement reads the cuvette at the main wavelength and again at a reference wavelength, then subtracts. Turbidity such as lipaemia, and a scratched or dirty cuvette, add nearly the same absorbance at both wavelengths, so the subtraction removes most of that. Haemolysis is not cancelled this way: free haemoglobin absorbs differently at the two wavelengths. Modern analysers measure a haemolysis index and flag the sample.

examples.question: An end-point glucose assay at 505 nm uses a 1 cm cuvette. A 5.0 mmol/L calibrator gives net A = 0.28; the sample gives net A = 0.42. Find glucose and the average cycle time at 600 tests per hour.
steps: Use c(sample) = c(std) × (A(sample) ÷ A(std)); A means net absorbance.
Cycle time = 3600 s ÷ 600 = 6 s on average.
examples.answer: Glucose is 7.5 mmol/L; average cycle time is 6 s.
examples.check:
c_std = 5.0
A_std = 0.28
A_sample = 0.42
c_sample = c_std * (A_sample / A_std)
print(c_sample)
print(3600 / 600)

traps: Using single-point calibration outside the linear range: the curve flattens, and a straight-line ratio under-reads the true concentration.
Reading a kinetic assay as an end point: absorbance is still changing; enzyme tests need ΔA/min.
Forgetting reagent carryover: a trace of previous reagent raises the next result; use an effective wash and check with a blank after a high-reagent sample, not by a reagent blank.
Mixing results from analysers with different wavelengths or path lengths: the same concentration gives a different absorbance.

quiz.q: List three wavelengths commonly selected by the filter wheel of a biochemical analyser.
quiz.a: 340 nm, 405 nm and 505 nm (also 546, 578 and 600 nm).

quiz.q: Why does an air-segmented continuous-flow analyser inject air bubbles into the stream?
quiz.a: Bubbles scrub the tube wall so sample does not smear, and they separate consecutive samples travelling to the single detector.

quiz.q: Why is the cuvette wheel held at 37 °C?
quiz.a: Enzyme rates are defined at body temperature; fixed 37 °C makes incubation reproducible and results comparable.

quiz.q: A calibrator of 4.0 mmol/L gives net A = 0.20 and a sample gives net A = 0.35. Find the sample concentration and the average cycle time at 900 tests per hour.
How does bichromatic measurement handle lipaemia, and why does it not correct haemolysis?
quiz.a: Lipaemia adds nearly the same absorbance at the main and reference wavelengths, so subtraction removes most of it. Haemolysis is not cancelled because free haemoglobin absorbs differently at the two wavelengths; modern analysers measure a haemolysis index and flag the sample.

quiz.q: A washed probe still holds a trace of the previous reagent. In which direction does the next patient's result shift, and how is it checked?
quiz.a: The next result shifts slightly upward. It is checked with a blank after a high-reagent sample and by watching the quality-control chart for a step.

beyond: Not for the exam. High-volume laboratories link analysers to a track with barcoded tubes; results release after rules-based checking. Many random-access analysers add an ion-selective electrode module for electrolytes. Search terms: random-access analyser, reagent carryover, Levey–Jennings chart, total laboratory automation, autoverification.
